Title: Anterior mediastinal nodular lesion segmentation from chest computed tomography imaging using UNet based neural network with attention mechanisms
Abstract: Automated detection of anterior mediastinal nodular lesions (AMLs) has significance for clinical usage as it is challenging for radiologists to accurately identify AMLs from chest computed tomography (CT) imaging due to various factors, including poor resolution, variations in intensity and the similarity of the AMLs to other tissues. To assist radiologists in AML detection from chest CT imaging, a UNet-based computer-aided detection (CADe) system is proposed to segment AMLs from slice images of the chest CT scans. The proposed network adopts a modified UNet architecture. To guide the proposed network to selectively focus on AMLs and potentially disregard others in the image, different attention mechanisms are utilized in the proposed network, including the self-attention mechanism and the convolutional block attention module (CBAM). The proposed network was trained and evaluated on 180 chest CT scans which consist of 180 AMLs. 90 AMLs were identified as thymic cysts, and 90 AMLs were diagnosed as thymoma. The proposed network achieved an average dice similarity coefficient (DSC) of 93.23 with 5-fold cross-validation, for which the mean Intersection over Union (IoU), sensitivity and specificity were 90.29, 93.98 and 95.68 respectively. Our method demonstrated an improved segmentation performance over state-of-the-art segmentation networks, including UNet, ResUNet, TransUNet and UNet++. The proposed network employing attention mechanisms exhibited a promising result for segmenting AMLs from chest CT imaging and could be used to automate the AML detection process for achieving improved diagnostic reliability.

gold.abstract: To automatically detect Anterior Mediastinum Lesions (AMLs) in the Anterior Mediastinum (AM), the primary requirement will be an automatic segmentation model specifically designed for the AM. The prevalence of AML is extremely low, making it challenging to conduct screening research similar to lung cancer screening. Retrospectively reviewing chest CT scans over a specific period to investigate the prevalence of AML requires substantial time. Therefore, developing an Artificial Intelligence (AI) model to find location of AM helps radiologist to enhance their ability to manage workloads and improve diagnostic accuracy for AMLs. In this paper, we introduce a U-shaped structure network to segment AM. Two attention mechanisms were used for maintaining long-range dependencies and localization. In order to have the potential of Multi-Head Self-Attention (MHSA) and a lightweight network, we designed a parallel MHSA named Wide-MHSA (W-MHSA). Maintaining long-range dependencies is crucial for segmentation when we upsample feature maps. Therefore, we designed a Dilated Depth-Wise Parallel Path connection (DDWPP) for this purpose. In order to design a lightweight architecture, we introduced an expanding convolution block and combine it with the proposed W-MHSA for feature extraction in the encoder part of the proposed U-shaped network. The proposed network was trained on 2775 AM cases, which obtained an average Dice Similarity Coefficient (DSC) of 87.83%, mean Intersection over Union (IoU) of 79.16%, and Sensitivity of 89.60%. Our proposed architecture exhibited superior segmentation performance compared to the most advanced segmentation networks, such as Trans Unet, Attention Unet, Res Unet, and Res Unet++.

Research task:
Develop a feasible and novel interdisciplinary research idea that genuinely integrates the two source papers. Specify the cross-disciplinary mechanism, a testable research design, and the contribution beyond either paper alone.

Source papers available to you:

These are your colleagues' latest proposals:

--- Researcher A ---
SOURCE CONTRIBUTIONS:
- Adopt from paper-b: attention-augmented UNet segments anterior mediastinal nodular lesions in chest CT; trained on 180 CTs with 180 AMLs (90 thymic cysts, 90 thymoma); DSC 93.23, IoU 90.29, sensitivity 93.98, specificity 95.68.
- Qualify colleague-reported paper-c: ACS 2023 lung screening criteria—ages 50–80, ≥20 pack-year, current/former smokers, annual low-dose CT, smoking-cessation linkage. Reject treating this as an independently verified source; accept only as an operational inclusion rule delivered by a colleague, pending confirmation.

INTEGRATION MECHANISM:
Apply paper-b’s attention UNet prospectively to low-dose CT from ACS-eligible individuals. The mechanistic link is not keyword overlap: screening eligibility defines a high-risk population, while paper-b’s attention maps provide a spatial prior for incidental AML detection. Attention is repurposed as an error-detection signal—if attention is low within a missed AML, the model flags uncertainty. This changes paper-b’s deployment from diagnostic CT to screening LDCT and links detection to population risk.

RESEARCH DESIGN:
Retrospective external cohort: 300 LDCT scans from ACS-eligible adults (50–80, ≥20 pack-year). Run the paper-b model; record Dice/IoU, sensitivity, specificity against radiologist ground truth for AMLs. Stratify performance by pack-year and comorbidity/life expectancy. Validate attention: compute mean attention within true AML vs background; test whether low attention predicts missed AMLs using AUROC. Primary outcome is incremental AML detection yield vs radiologist-only read; secondary outcomes are cyst-overdiagnosis rate and smoking-cessation referral linkage.

WORKING ABSTRACT:
We propose deploying paper-b’s attention UNet within an ACS guideline-defined high-risk lung-screening LDCT cohort to test whether attention-weighted AML segmentation improves risk-stratified detection and informs overdiagnosis and cessation decisions. Missing cross-paper knowledge: the paper-c abstract is unavailable, so guideline criteria remain colleague-reported and require source verification.

FINAL IDEA: Integrate paper-b’s attention UNet into ACS guideline-selected low-dose CT screening to test whether attention maps improve incidental AML detection and risk-stratified overdiagnosis assessment.

--- Researcher B ---
SOURCE CONTRIBUTIONS:
- Paper-c (ACS 2023 guideline): annual low-dose CT (LDCT) for ages 50–80 with ≥20 pack-years; shared decision-making; smoking-cessation linkage; comorbidity/life-expectancy limits screening.
- Paper-b (colleague-reported, not independently verified): attention-augmented UNet segments anterior mediastinal nodular lesions on chest CT, distinguishing thymic cysts from thymoma (DSC 93.23, sensitivity 93.98 in 180 CTs). Original paper-b full text unavailable.

INTEGRATION MECHANISM:
Do not use paper-b to detect primary lung nodules; it targets mediastinal lesions. Instead, embed paper-b’s attention UNet into paper-c’s LDCT screening pathway to triage incidental anterior mediastinal findings. The UNet’s segmentation/classification output becomes a shared-decision-making input, reducing unnecessary follow-up while preserving paper-c’s harm–benefit logic. This operationally links AI lesion classification to screening guideline decisions.

RESEARCH DESIGN:
Retrospective cohort of ACS-eligible LDCT screens with incidental anterior mediastinal lesions. Fine-tune paper-b’s attention UNet on LDCT data, with pathology/radiologist consensus as ground truth. Measure segmentation DSC/IoU, cyst-vs-thymoma AUC, sensitivity/specificity. Validate on external LDCT set. Primary outcome: proportion of cases where UNet output changes ACS-informed follow-up recommendation; secondary outcomes: avoided biopsies, false-positive referrals, time to diagnosis, and attention-map radiologist interpretability. Missing cross-paper knowledge: paper-b’s original CT dose/field strength and external generalizability must be confirmed.

WORKING ABSTRACT:
This project couples ACS lung-cancer screening with an attention UNet for anterior mediastinal lesions. Rather than replacing lung-nodule detection, the model triages incidental mediastinal findings on screening LDCT, feeding its classification into shared decision-making. The design tests whether this reduces unnecessary invasive follow-up without delaying thymoma diagnosis, transferring AI segmentation into population screening harm reduction.

FINAL IDEA: Use paper-b’s attention UNet to classify incidental anterior mediastinal lesions on ACS lung-cancer screening LDCT as a shared-decision-making triage tool that reduces unnecessary follow-up while preserving early thymoma detection.

High-uncertainty AMLs trigger radiologist review or shortened follow-up; low-uncertainty cyst classifications support conservative management, directly modifying shared decision-making and potential overdiagnosis.

Fine-tune paper-b’s attention UNet on this LDCT AML set; perform 5-fold cross-validation. Measure DSC/IoU, sensitivity/specificity, cyst-vs-thymoma AUC. Compare triage outcomes—unnecessary biopsy rate, delayed thymoma diagnosis, number needed to review—against ACS default follow-up using decision-curve analysis; track smoking-cessation referral linkage.

WORKING ABSTRACT:
We embed paper-b’s attention UNet into ACS-guided LDCT screening to triage incidental anterior mediastinal lesions. Attention-derived uncertainty flags cases needing review, while low-uncertainty cyst classifications reduce invasive follow-up. Validation combines segmentation accuracy, attention-error detection, and net benefit over standard screening pathway. Missing cross-paper knowledge: paper-c’s full guideline text is not available; all paper-c claims remain colleague-reported.
